newsitem.title: GERMANY: Chechen sympathiser in Germany jailed for hijack.
newsitem.headline: Chechen sympathiser in Germany jailed for hijack.

text.p: A Bavarian court sentenced a Turkish waiter on Monday to six years and ten months in jail after he confessed to hijacking a plane with a toy gun to win sympathy for the Chechen separatists in Russia.

A court in the Bavarian town of Landshut found Ramazan Aydin, 21, guilty of holding up a North Cyprus Turkish Airlines Boeing 727 flying from northern Cyprus to Istanbul with 108 crew and passengers on board, and diverting it to Munich last March.

The court ruled that Aydin's use of a toy gun and fake explosives counted in his favour and rejected the prosecution's demand for seven years and three months in jail. It accepted his defence during the three-day hearing that he had not intended to harm those on board.
Aydin said that as a devout Moslem he merely wanted to help his "Chechen brothers" and that he hoped his act would prompt European states to intervene to end the conflict in Russia.
Speaking in Turkish through a translator, he accepted the court's decision and said he regretted the suffering caused to his 108 hostages during their 11-hour ordeal.

"But it must not be forgotten that thousands of Moslem brothers have been killed in Chechnya and I was only fighting for their freedom," Aydin said, referring to the 21-month conflict between Chechen separatists and Russian forces.
Moscow agreed on a truce with Chechen rebels in August.
"I implore you to hang a picture of me in a square in Munich that says that this man defended the freedom of others," he appealed to the court.
Aydin was tried under juvenile law because he was 20 years old when he held up the plane. The maximum penalty for an adult convicted of hijacking in Germany is 15 years in jail.

After Aydin surrendered and freed his hostages at Munich airport, Bavarian police said had duped authorities in several countries for 11 hours into believing three more armed hijackers were also on board.
Aydin had told the court that he and a friend had visited Chechnya, an autonomous republic in southern Russia, without Russian visas on what he described as a "pirate ship" in the summer of 1995.
He described how they witnessed atrocities committed during the conflict between Russian forces and Chechen rebels and that his friend was later killed in the Chechen capital Grozny.
